title: Symptom-Level Comorbidity Patterns Between Depression and Internet Gaming Disorder Among Adolescents: Evidence from Longitudinal Network Analysis with Gender Considerations
authors: Shiyun Chen, Yue Zhao, Xinli Chi, Shimin Zhu
abstract: Adolescence is a period with an increased risk for the co-occurrence of depression and Internet gaming disorder (IGD), yet we still know little about how specific symptoms of these two conditions influence each other over time. In this study, we applied cross-lagged panel network analysis to two-wave data from a community sample of 538 adolescents (Mean age = 12.51 years; 53.7 percent female). Potential gender differences in the network structure were examined. In the overall sample and in both gender groups, depressive symptoms consistently predicted later gaming-related problems, whereas no reverse cross-disorder pathways were retained. In particular, suicidal ideation and psychomotor symptoms emerged as bridge symptoms linking depression and IGD, while sleep problems showed moderate outgoing expected influence in the overall symptom network. While boys and girls showed broadly similar patterns, some differences emerged in how specific symptoms were connected and which symptoms were most influential. These findings clarify the longitudinal symptom-level associations between depression and IGD in adolescents, suggesting that addressing key depressive symptoms may help reduce the risk of later IGD.

title: Artificial intelligence and journalism in Ibero-America: A comparative study of perceptions, practices and challenges
authors: Paulo Nuno Vicente, Sara Pérez-Seijo, Suzana Barbosa
abstract: This article explores the perceptions, practices, challenges and opportunities associated with the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in journalistic practice within the Ibero-American context. Drawing on an original quantitative comparative study conducted in Portugal, Spain and Brazil, the research investigates how professional journalists understand, engage with and respond to the integration of AI-driven tools in newsrooms. Based on survey data from 271 journalists, the findings reveal widespread but predominantly basic knowledge of AI, general curiosity and cautious optimism regarding its implementation, and notable concern about its impact on professional ethics, job security, and editorial transparency. The study highlights significant variations across countries in the use of AI applications. Key challenges identified include the absence of formal editorial guidelines, limited training opportunities and a lack of transparency in the use of AI-generated content. The research underscores the urgent need for institutional strategies that ensure responsible AI integration, safeguard journalistic standards and support professional development.

title: Trending by design: How algorithmic activists amplified and recalibrated an elite anti-Ukrainian campaign on X
abstract: The ability of far-right actors to manipulate social media traffic sparks concerns over the quality of public discourse. Although the scholarship on far-right digital activism has established its role in aiding elite communication, we know little about mechanisms through which such campaigns are amplified and recalibrated in the process. This article addresses this gap through the lens of algorithmic activism, investigating how digital activists leveraged platform features to amplify and recalibrate the elite-initiated campaign #StopUkrainizacjiPolski on X. Combining descriptive statistics, social network analysis and critical discourse analysis, we examine 130,788 posts from February 2022 to September 2024. Findings demonstrate that a small group of accounts amplified the hashtag by hijacking the X trending board while recalibrating campaign objectives via indexical linkages to other hashtags, invoking instrumental pacifism, historical grievances, and antisemitic conspiracy theories. The study elucidates how platform affordances shape how digital activists engage in elite campaigns with implications for the reach and form of exclusionary discourse.

title: The challenge of AI dependence: exploring its impact on cognitive autonomy and elaboration in creative performance
authors: Yanyang Ma, Kerun Li, Yulei Liu
abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

title: Diminishing returns to calibrated reliance on AI: effects on deliverable quality and rework effort, moderated by task verifiability
authors: Junjie Sun, Yifan Yang, Jiangnan Cheng, Weichao Ding
abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can function as both “performance accelerators” and “risk propagators” in organizations. This study investigates how AI-enabled work capability, particularly employees' decomposition and evaluation skills, is associated with deliverable quality and rework effort through the behavioral pathway of calibrated reliance on AI. Additionally, it examines task verifiability as a critical boundary condition that shapes the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration. Design/methodology/approach Guided by appropriate reliance and automation trust theories, data from 380 workers were analyzed using SmartPLS 4 (partial least squares structural equation modeling) and hierarchical polynomial regression to test mediation, moderation, and quadratic effects. Procedural remedies and a latent method factor approach were employed to assess common method bias. Findings AI-enabled work capability was positively associated with calibrated reliance on AI. Calibrated reliance on AI was associated with higher deliverable quality and lower rework effort. A double diminishing marginal pattern emerged: as reliance calibration increased, quality gains and rework reductions leveled off, indicating a “too-much-of-a-good-thing” pattern. Task verifiability strengthened the positive association between calibrated reliance and deliverable quality and also strengthened its negative association with rework effort. Originality/value This study shifts the focus from reliance intensity to reliance calibration in explaining AI-enabled work outcomes. It documents a double diminishing marginal pattern, showing that the benefits of calibrated reliance are meaningful but not unlimited. It also identifies task verifiability as a boundary condition that helps explain when calibrated reliance is more strongly associated with improved deliverable quality and reduced rework effort. These findings provide focused guidance for capability development, reliance calibration, and task-specific AI governance.

title: Augmentation or automation? A dual-path model of GenAI usage motivations and employee creativity
authors: Yujie Shi, Jiang Xu, Jih-Yu Mao, Minya Xu
abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can both enhance and constrain employee creativity, yet the mechanisms underlying these divergent effects remain unclear. This study examines how augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage shape employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on dual-process theory and self-regulation theory, we distinguish augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage and propose distinct cognitive mechanisms linking them to creativity. We test the hypotheses using a multi-wave, multi-source field survey and a scenario-based experiment. Findings Augmentation motivation is positively associated with employee creativity through knowledge integration, whereas automation motivation is negatively related to creativity through knowledge dependence. Conscientiousness strengthens the positive indirect effect of augmentation motivation and attenuates the negative indirect effect of automation motivation on employee creativity. Research limitations/implications Augmentation and automation motivations may coexist and vary across tasks and use episodes. Future research could explore these dynamics, examine how other individual differences shape their effects, and assess whether the consequences of GenAI dependence vary across work contexts. Practical implications Organizations should encourage employees to use GenAI to generate and develop ideas rather than replace their own judgment. Training could help employees critically assess AI-generated suggestions and combine them with their own knowledge. Originality/value This research shifts attention from how much employees use GenAI to why they use it. By distinguishing augmentation and automation motivations, it explains when and why GenAI can enhance or constrain employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms.

title: The AI trust paradox: how disclosure, brand authenticity and consumer mindset shape communication effectiveness
abstract: Purpose This study investigates the trust paradox in artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content, where efficiency conflicts with perceived inauthenticity. Integrating source credibility theory and congruity theory, it examines how the interplay between ad genesis (AI vs. genuine), strategic context (disclosure, brand authenticity) and consumer mindset (construal level) determines communication effectiveness. Design/methodology/approach A three-study experimental design was employed to isolate specific contingencies. Study 1 manipulated ad genesis and AI disclosure to test engagement. Study 2 examined the moderating role of brand authenticity on purchase intentions. Study 3 tested the congruity between AI message focus (hedonic vs. utilitarian) and consumer construal levels. Findings Genuine imagery generally outperforms AI-generated imagery; however, effectiveness is contingent on strategic fit. Disclosure boosts engagement for genuine ads but reduces it for AI content. AI ads enhance purchase intentions for low-authenticity brands but damage high-authenticity ones. Furthermore, hedonic AI appeals align with high-construal mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit low-construal consumers. Research limitations/implications The experiments used static images in controlled online settings. Future research should test dynamic and multimodal AI content and validate the effects with real-world behavioral metrics, such as click-through and conversion rates. Practical implications AI use should fit the context. Heritage brands should avoid AI imagery, whereas challenger brands can benefit from it. Disclosure helps genuine-image ads but hurts AI-generated ads. Hedonic AI appeals suit abstract mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit concrete mindsets. Originality/value This research advances advertising theory by applying a split-credibility lens to AI-generated advertising, demonstrating that effectiveness depends on source-context congruence.

title: The Political Leaning of Fact-Checking: Countering Italian Disinformation on the War in Ukraine
abstract: The intense disinformation efforts that accompanied Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine highlight the importance of countering misinformation to mitigate the influence of foreign actors, particularly in vulnerable public spheres such as the Italian one. Despite widespread use, the effectiveness of fact-checking in correcting misinformation remains ambiguous, with limited exploration of the underlying reasons. This article focuses on the role of political leaning and partisanship in shaping individuals’ comprehension of factual information, their inclination to fact-checking exposure, and their capacity to assimilate findings that challenge their preconceived beliefs. We measure the role of these variables for 10 different statements about Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, employing original survey data collected in Italy in spring 2022. We find veracity assessment to be associated with partisan views of the war for both true and false statements, with Russia-leaning views frequently correlating with lower exposure to and reception of fact-checks. Right-leaning political attitudes often work in the same direction, in some cases amplifying the partisan rejection of fact-checks. These findings contribute to literature on fact-checking, selective exposure, motivated reasoning, and misinformation, corroborating previous studies on the limits of debunking efforts and extending their insights to a setting well known for its high level of political parallelism. A crucial implication of these results is that political attitudes should receive greater consideration when addressing misinformation and foreign disinformation efforts, given their potential to amplify partisan barriers that moderate the corrective power of fact-checking. Furthermore, this partisan acceptance of fact-checks complicates the normative assessment of journalistic practices.

title: Counterspeech or Disagreement? Comparing Oppositional Replies in China’s AI Controversies on Social Media
abstract: Online technological controversies often involve both ordinary disagreement and counterspeech, yet these forms of opposition are rarely compared within the same discussion environment. Drawing on argumentation theories, this study compares disagreement replies to non-hateful comments with counterspeech replies to hateful comments in Douyin discussions of China’s AI controversies, where hate speech may include stigmatizing generalizations about social groups. Using 9,407 oppositional parent–response dyads, we compared like counts, toxicity, subsequent toxic replies, and the distribution and reception of six response types. Counterspeech and disagreement did not differ significantly in like counts, but counterspeech exhibited higher toxicity and was related to greater odds of toxicity among direct replies posted within seven days. Despite sharing the same six response types, the two response contexts varied in their type distributions and associations with likes. These findings situate counterspeech within a broader spectrum of online opposition, revealing contextual differences in its argumentative expression and subsequent interaction across hateful and non-hateful contexts.

title: When availability is not enough: Content prominence and diversity on a public service VoD platform
abstract: As public service media (PSM) shift from broadcasting to video on demand (VoD), prominence has become a key mechanism through which public value is operationalised. While policy debates emphasise the visibility of culturally significant content, evidence on how interface prominence shapes viewing remains scarce. Building on theories of affordances, prominence, and media diversity, this article conceptualises diversity transformation as the process through which diversity changes from catalogue availability, through interface prominence, to audience consumption. Using a longitudinal dataset from Estonian Public Broadcasting (ERR), the study finds that prominence and premieres are the strongest predictors of VoD viewing, explaining 62 per cent of the variance. The findings illustrate a process of diversity transformation: Although ERR’s VoD catalogue is diverse, interface prominence and audience consumption become concentrated around scripted and foreign titles. The study confirms that the VoD interface has become a strategic site where PSM negotiate tensions between universality, cultural responsibility, and audience demand.

title: Rasch Analysis of the Korean Internet Social Capital Scales
abstract: Internet‐based ties increasingly function as social resources, but item‐ and category‐level evidence for the Korean Internet Social Capital Scales (K‐ISCS) remains limited. This study evaluated the 18‐item, 7‐point K‐ISCS using Rasch measurement in a nationwide online panel of Korean adults ( n = 1500). Residual‐based dimensionality diagnostics supported the theoretical distinction between online bonding and bridging social capital; therefore, the main analyses were conducted separately by subscale. Both subscales showed generally acceptable item fit, ordered category functioning, high person reliability and separation, and precisely estimated item difficulty hierarchies within the calibration sample. Item 4 in the bonding subscale and item 18 in the bridging subscale showed underfit, indicating the need for closer review of the emergency‐loan and frequent‐new‐contact items. Person–item maps and test information functions showed that both subscales measured most precisely near the center of the latent continuum, with lower precision at the tails. DIF was mostly negligible across gender and age groups, although item 18 showed slight‐to‐moderate gender‐related DIF. Overall, the findings support interpreting the K‐ISCS as two related but distinct subscales for assessing perceived online bonding and bridging resources in Korean adults, rather than as an undifferentiated total score.

title: Fandom Rupture in the Movement Society: Reactive Collective Participation Through Affective Practices
abstract: When an external shock draws heterogeneous actors into a single platform arena before any collective aim emerges, participation persists at movement-like intensity. Existing theories have not specified the cohering mechanism through which this formation sustains. This study conceptualizes this mode as reactive collective participation and specifies how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at the practice level. A mixed-methods design integrates in-depth interviews with 13 heterogeneously positioned participants (fans, anti-fans, bystanders) and computational analysis of Weibo discourse surrounding the 2023 Cai Xukun scandal (139,795 posts; 205,001 comments). Four affective practices recur across the event: Positioning, Storying, Attunement, and Calibration. These practices shift in relative weight across the event’s life cycle and distribute unevenly across actor positions, producing a stratified ecology in which insulated defense and exposed antagonism sustain each other. The study advances affective publics theory by specifying how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at practice level, and collective participation theory by conceptualizing reactive collective participation as a mode that reconnects the movement society and fan activism frameworks through a reactive pathway.

title: Reframing moderation: Frame moderation as a radical-right party strategy
abstract: Many radical-right parties across Western Europe have normalized electorally while holding stable, hardline positions on immigration. This paper argues that these parties have moderated the perception of their core policies not through positional moderation, but through frame moderation: they change how they justify a policy without necessarily changing the policy itself, altering the considerations through which voters perceive their position. Conceptually, the paper distinguishes the range of frames a party invokes from the frequency with which it invokes these frames. Empirically, it develops a scalable measure of framing width and of change within frame categories using a novel method of sentence embeddings. Its usefulness is illustrated with the case of the French National Rally’s framing of immigration across manifestos from 1997 to 2022. As the party normalized, it widened its range of frames, increased its framing of immigration in terms of economic considerations, and moved from a cultural frame that emphasized ethnic homogeneity toward one that focuses on the defense of secularism and gender equality. Frame moderation enables stigmatized parties to appear more mainstream without moderating their positions. This suggests that positional measures alone may understate how radical-right parties have changed.

title: Delayed Date and Motivated Vote: How Election Postponement Shapes Turnout
abstract: Autocracies postpone elections for political control, but we lack an understanding of how voters respond to election postponement in autocracies. This paper argues that election postponement motivates voter turnout across partisan groups, because voters see the postponement as a sign of regime weakness and increased electoral competitiveness. Evidence from a survey experiment in Hong Kong demonstrates that reminder messages about election postponement motivate various partisan groups to turn out, an effect robust to whether and how the message is framed. While the turnout effect is larger when the message’s narrative aligns with the subject’s partisanship—such as the propaganda and intimidation frames for government supporters and the electioneering frame for opposition supporters—all postponement reminder messages have an average turnout effect, with no significant differences across partisan groups. These findings suggest that election postponement is consequential in shaping citizens’ political behavior, with crucial implications for election turnout and authoritarian stability.

title: Affective dynamics of welfare chauvinism under different policy funding structures
abstract: This research investigates how distinct emotional responses to immigrants—namely, compassion, anger, and anxiety—are connected to welfare chauvinist attitudes within varying welfare policy funding contexts. Leveraging Turkey's experience with large‐scale immigration and the exogenous nature of EU funding, a population‐representative survey experiment was conducted, manipulating claimant identity (native vs. immigrant) and the funding source of welfare assistance (state vs. EU‐funded). Results show that a “care deficit” operates as a key mechanism linking immigrant identity and lower support for immigrant welfare access, but only within the nation‐bound welfare system. Once compassion is evoked, however, it operates similarly for natives and immigrants. Furthermore, moderation analyses reveal divergent patterns of compassion, anger, and anxiety in shaping welfare chauvinist attitudes across different policy funding structures. Highlighting the crucial interplay between emotions and the policy funding schemes in which welfare assistance is delivered, this research contributes to the debate on what drives welfare chauvinism. Drawing on the political psychology literature, this study offers a perspective on the emotional dynamics associated with the persistent native‐immigrant welfare support gap and discusses potential factors that may contribute to narrowing this disparity.

title: Democratic hypocrisy: support for undemocratic responses to protest in Germany
authors: Morgan Le Corre Juratic, Markus Wagner, Daniel Bischof
abstract: Political tolerance is a cornerstone of liberal democracy, yet citizens apply it selectively: intolerance is higher for disliked groups. However, does this extend to democratic hypocrisy, leading to support for undemocratic responses to protest? We address this important question through a vignette survey experiment ( N  = 5,000) in Germany, comparing reactions to similar protest tactics used by farmers and climate activists in a realistic, externally valid setting. We show that respondents were not only less willing to grant climate activists key democratic rights but also significantly more likely to support undemocratic responses to climate protesters, including imprisonment without trial. Our findings underline that citizens engage in democratic hypocrisy: their political biases lead them to support undemocratic actions against disliked groups.

title: Comparing belief certainty formats in the measurement of political knowledge
abstract: Psychological certainty plays a role in how respondents retrieve and express their attitudes, beliefs, and opinions. This study compares two question formats that allow respondents to express certainty about their political knowledge. Using a YouGov sample ( N = 2,161), a single-item certainty-in-knowledge format, where political knowledge and belief certainty are measured jointly, and a branching format, where knowledge is measured first, followed by certainty in a separate question, are compared. The results show that the certainty-in-knowledge format significantly reduces the likelihood of respondents looking up answers online. Including a “Don’t Know” option does not increase gender differences. These findings demonstrate a question format that improves validity in online surveys by reducing measurement artifacts.

title: Automatically Coding Economic Activities via Semantic Search
abstract: Automated coding of free-text descriptions is a core challenge for National Statistical Institutes (NSIs), which must map colloquial respondent inputs to official taxonomies under strict reliability and transparency requirements. Rule-based systems, the current standard, demand extensive, ongoing human effort to author and maintain the large manual rule sets needed to cover the diversity of real world inputs. This paper evaluates embedding-based semantic retrieval as a lower-maintenance alternative, using the Italian ATECO classification as the empirical setting. We compare several knowledge base construction strategies across seven sentence transformer models (ranging from 118 million to 8 billion parameters), evaluated against 33,544 real-world queries labelled by CIRCE, Istat’s operational rule-based coder, at the 5-digit and 2-digit levels. Moderate-size models (300–700 million parameters) are competitive with much larger ones, achieving Hit@5 above 0.82 and 0.94 at the respective levels. Query length is a significant performance driver, and manual mismatch analysis reveals that roughly one in five disagreements with CIRCE reflect label noise rather than retrieval errors. Embedding-based retrieval thus offers competitive performance with no task-specific training data and a fraction of the human labour required by rule-based approaches.

title: A Typology of Live Video Interviewing Paradata: Understanding, Collecting, and Leveraging Paradata to Improve Survey Data Quality
authors: Sebastian Kocar, Andrew L Hupp, Gabriele Durrant, Tim Hanson, Matt Brown
abstract: The adoption of live video interviewing (VI) was limited until the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Since then, uptake has increased with methodological research focusing primarily on VI implementation and its implications for data quality, including response rates, representation, and measurement error. However, the collection and use of paradata describing the process of survey data collection within this emerging mode has so far received little attention. This study addresses this gap by developing and presenting a new typology of VI paradata aligned with the Total Survey Error (TSE) framework, which encompasses paradata from across all survey stages, including pre-data collection, recruitment, video platform, interview process, and post-interview paradata. The article presents good practices for VI paradata collection and application and is the first to systematically discuss paradata associated with the VI process. The evidence presented is based on a scoping review and critical assessment of surveys that collected VI paradata. From the scoping review, it is clear that the collection of VI paradata has thus far been limited to a relatively narrow range, has likely not been strategically planned, and the resulting paradata have generally been underused. Our comprehensive review and synthesis demonstrate that VI paradata from different survey phases have the potential to be effectively applied to assess survey data in different ways. Combined with a discussion of new examples of VI paradata, including those supported by the use of (integrated) video platforms or by artificial intelligence (AI), this study provides important evidence of how VI paradata can enhance future survey practice. The recommendation is that survey researchers should adopt a strategic, comprehensive, innovative, and empirically grounded approach to VI paradata collection and use, in order to maximize the potential of this emerging data collection mode.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Theory-Aligned Social Science Content Analysis: Evidence From Collaborative Learning Discourse
authors: Yoonhee Shin, Youngkwan Son, Haengkyung Lee, Minyoung Kim
abstract: Theory-based content analysis is central to social science research, but coding context-dependent interactional discourse remains difficult to scale. This study examines whether fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) can support theory-aligned, episode-level coding of complex social interaction, using socially shared metacognitive regulation (SSMR) in collaborative learning discourse as a demanding empirical case. Using a human-coded dataset of 2,372 discourse episodes from undergraduate collaborative problem-solving, we adapted the large language model content analysis (LACA) framework through an AI-aligned codebook, prompt design, and supervised fine-tuning. Prompt-only and fine-tuned models were compared across episode-level classification and multilayer SSMR coding. Fine-tuned models substantially improved agreement with human coding and predictive performance relative to prompt-only baselines. Performance was strongest for episode-level classification and several higher-support coding layers, whereas errors remained concentrated in sparse, boundary-prone, and highly interpretive categories requiring social-intent reconstruction and temporally unfolding context. The findings extend recent work on LLM-assisted qualitative and content analysis by showing both the promise and limits of supervised, theory-aligned automation for multilayer social interaction coding. Overall, the study supports a human-centered approach to LLM-assisted content analysis, in which automated coding can support more stable coding tasks while human expertise remains essential for ambiguous, boundary-prone, and interpretively demanding judgments.

title: A practical guide to self-organising maps in psychological research
authors: Ido Shalev, Estherina Trachtenberg, Maria B. Jelen, William Mills, Marc Bennett, Rebecca P. Lawson, Tim Dalgleish, Duncan E. Astle
abstract: Identifying shared and distinct profiles, whether of symptoms, personality traits, or cognitive abilities, is essential for understanding psychological phenomena, yet doing so requires navigating interrelated theoretical, conceptual, and technical complexities. First, most psychological phenomena typically exist along continuous spectra rather than discrete categories, complicating the characterisation of inherently heterogeneous constructs. Second, studying individual differences requires balancing population-level generalisation with person-level interpretability, which is critical for applied science and clinical practice. Third, psychological data often contain missing values, non-linear relationships, and high-dimensional patterns that violate standard statistical assumptions. Commonly used approaches for profile detection often fall short of these demands, producing oversimplified or difficult-to-interpret results that are hard to map back to the individual. In contrast, self-organising maps (SOMs) offer a powerful, visual, and intuitive solution that addresses these challenges. Despite growing interest, SOMs remain underutilised in psychology, likely due to a lack of accessible tutorials and clear guidelines tailored to the field. This tutorial introduces SOMs to psychologists without technical backgrounds, emphasising practical implementation. We provide evidence-based recommendations for key methodological decisions, accompanied by annotated R code. Using a dataset of depressive symptoms as an illustrative case, we present a complete workflow covering data preprocessing, map initialisation, parameter optimisation, and interpretation. We further discuss advanced SOM extensions relevant to psychological research and highlight key limitations of the method. By making SOMs accessible, this tutorial supports nuanced, person-centred analyses that preserve the complexity of psychological phenomena.

title: The Brief Transprejudice Scale: Development and Validation
authors: Diana Cheso, R. Thora Bjornsdottir, Ryan McKay, Hanna Zagef ka
abstract: In recent years, research on predictors of transprejudice has increased, yet existing psychometric measures of the construct have limitations, including outdated terminology, conflation of gender atypicality with trans identity and a lack of multidimensional structure. We report on the development and validation of the Brief Transprejudice Scale (BTS), a concise yet multifaceted measure of transprejudice. In Study 1 ( N = 341), exploratory factor analysis and Rasch analysis were used to refine an initial item pool, resulting in a three-factor (negative affect, category exclusion and moralism) 14-item scale . In Study 2 ( N = 391), confirmatory factor analysis supported this factor structure, and validity tests demonstrated the scale’s strong concurrent, convergent and divergent validity. Despite its brevity, this new scale provides a psychometrically sound and efficient tool that allows researchers to capture multiple aspects of transprejudice.

title: Increasing Support for Humanitarian Aid to Palestinian Civilians During the Israel–Gaza War Through Ideologically Tailored Social-Media Campaigns
abstract: Promoting support for humanitarian aid to an adversarial outgroup is difficult during active war. We introduce a digital field-experimental approach that embeds psychologically grounded interventions in people’s actual social-media environments. During the Israel–Gaza war, 6,105 adult Jewish Israeli Facebook users were assigned to a no-study-campaign control condition, a humanitarian-moral campaign emphasizing humanitarian obligation, or an instrumental-security campaign presenting aid as advancing Israeli security. Days after the campaigns ended, 4,784 participants completed the follow-up survey. Support for humanitarian aid declined in the control condition but increased under both campaigns, suggesting that psychological social-media interventions can buffer or reverse erosion of humanitarian attitudes during acute conflict. Political ideology moderated relative effectiveness: the instrumental-security campaign was especially effective among conservatives, whereas liberals responded positively to both. These findings provide partial support for ideological message matching and offer a scalable, ecologically valid framework for testing intergroup interventions in real-world settings.

title: People know who to ask for favors despite underestimating compliance
authors: Casher D. Belinda, Brittany C. Solomon
abstract: Whether and how people approach social interactions hinges on how they expect others to respond. Extensive social psychology research suggests that people are inaccurate interpersonal perceivers, overestimating negative responses (e.g., discomfort) and underestimating positive responses (e.g., appreciation) across a variety of social situations. However, this conclusion is based almost exclusively on mean-level bias analyses that obscure the dyadic nature of interpersonal judgment and rely on a narrow conceptualization of interpersonal accuracy. Leveraging research on favor-asking and anticipated compliance as an exemplar, we demonstrate that interpersonal accuracy takes multiple theoretically distinct forms, and that the prevailing conclusion that people misunderstand their influence over others—because they tend to underestimate compliance—is likely overgeneralized. Across four studies (13,196 directed dyadic ratings), we show that people accurately differentiate between who will comply with their favor requests (dyadic meta-accuracy) despite the average tendency to underestimate compliance (mean-level bias). This pattern emerged for specific and general favor requests, among well- and newly-acquainted individuals, and beyond what could be expected due to self-projection. Through this dyadic lens, people are highly adept judges of their influence over others, as they are able to target their requests toward individuals who are uniquely likely to acquiesce to them—and can avoid wasting time on those who are not. Thus, our research refines existing implications for how people approach asking for favors. More broadly, by aligning theory, measurement, and level of analysis, our studies elucidate the need for greater theoretical precision and empirical breadth in interpersonal accuracy research.
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

title: Belonging to a group with shared ideology leads preschool children to resist revising their beliefs despite disconfirming evidence
abstract: Shared beliefs can bring people together but may motivate prioritizing group affiliation over facts supported by evidence. Indeed, affiliation with a group whose membership is tied to shared beliefs (i.e., ideology-based groups) has led adults to endorse and maintain false beliefs. We demonstrate that this resistance to revise beliefs that form the basis of group membership has its origins in childhood. In three studies, 4- to 5-y-old children ( N = 192 ) endorse a claim about a novel causal system and subsequently join a group that shares their endorsement. Children randomly assigned to a focal Belief-contingent condition learn that their membership in the group is based on this claim, framed as a shared belief. We contrast this with conditions where group members hold the same shared belief, but this belief is not a condition for group membership (Experiments 1, 2, and 3), and where group members hold to the same claim framed as a “guess” (Experiment 2). After joining a group, children see evidence that their initial endorsement was incorrect and then have an opportunity to revise based on the new information. Only when group membership was contingent on the shared belief did children hold on to (and act on—Experiment 3) their initial incorrect endorsement. These findings suggest that the affiliative power of ideology has developmental roots; even in our earliest years, affiliative motives override truth-seeking and rationality. Thus, our early-emerging motive to identify with groups may underlie later cases of evidence denial and polarization.
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
